name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,383

clue.text: Pillbox maybe contained illicit drugs, including ecstasy

indicators.note: including something means taking it inside, so the drug letter goes within the first word

blocks.note: to have contained something is to have had it
E is the street abbreviation for the drug ecstasy
gear is slang for illegal drugs

explanation.surface: A pillbox of contraband turns out to hold illegal drugs, ecstasy among them.
explanation.walkthrough: A pillbox is a small round brimless hat, not a container for pills; gear is British slang for drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A pillbox hat is one example of something worn on the head, hence 'maybe' marking an example.

clue.text: Rush job

blocks.note: first meaning: to hurtle along at speed
second meaning: a person's working life or profession

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rush job' reads as a hurried piece of work, but the two words are separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for moving fast and out of control and also a noun for a lifelong profession.

clue.text: Holes in one area dry up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for area
sec describes dry wine

explanation.surface: A golfer's holes in one in a drought-hit area are drying up.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf an ace is a hole completed with a single stroke, so a plural of that term means several such holes.

clue.text: Pizza's topping has various items (no peppers)

indicators.note: the topping of a word in a down clue is its first letter, the one at the top
various suggests things in a mixed, varied arrangement, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
the two words supply the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A menu note: this pizza's topping comes with assorted ingredients but no peppers.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket hides the definition: 'no' belongs to the anagram and 'peppers' is the answer, the opposite of what the surface says.
explanation.definitionFit: Pimentos are sweet red peppers, often stuffed into olives, so the plural matches the plural noun directly.

clue.text: Decide when American leaves a place in Washington

indicators.note: when something leaves a word, those letters are taken out of it

blocks.note: Seattle is the largest city in Washington state
A is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Someone decides on the move once an American has left a city in Washington.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the A from SEATTLE to leave SETTLE. 'Washington' suggests the US capital but here it is the north-western state.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle a question or dispute is to resolve it finally, a common synonym for deciding.

clue.text: Pop star, having acquired stock, may be this rich

definitions.note: the answer is an intensifier, as in the phrase 'stinking rich'

indicators.note: having acquired something means taking it in, so one word is placed inside the other

blocks.note: Sting is the stage name of the singer from the Police
stock in the sense of family lineage or relatives

explanation.surface: A pop star who has bought shares on the stock market may become extremely wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock' looks financial but means ancestry; the definition is the phrase the answer completes, as in the idiom for being enormously wealthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Stinking is an informal intensifier meaning extremely, used most often in the idiom for being enormously wealthy.

clue.text: Kid is the first person in Paris to get fine

indicators.note: the French word gets, or takes in, another word inside itself

blocks.note: je is French for I, the first person pronoun
OK means fine or acceptable

explanation.surface: A child is the first person in Paris to be fined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid' looks like a noun for a child, but it is the verb meaning to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: To kid someone is to tease or fool them playfully, which is what you do when you jest with them.

clue.text: Very big wardrobes, excluding trousers

indicators.note: used as a verb, trousers means pockets or takes in, so the answer is held inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Very large wardrobes that leave out trousers, a clothing description.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trousers' looks like clothing in a wardrobe but is the verb meaning pockets.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese describes a person who is extremely overweight, a clinical word for being very large in body.

clue.text: Plan to transform the Arctic

indicators.note: to transform something is to change its form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: both words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A scheme to change the Arctic, perhaps by melting or development.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to architect means to design or devise a scheme, just as planning something does.

clue.text: Want 50% less antagonism

indicators.note: half the word is kept, here its first two of four letters

blocks.note: to want something is to need it
the front half of the word

explanation.surface: A wish for half as much hostility.
explanation.definitionFit: Needle in British informal use means hostility or provocation, especially between sporting rivals.

clue.text: Extremely slow intake is worrying

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two end letters

blocks.note: the first and last letters
food intake is eating

explanation.surface: Someone eating extremely slowly is a cause for concern.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweating informally means being anxious or nervous about something, as in sweating over exam results.

clue.text: Message misspelling detailed legal term

indicators.note: read as de-tailed, the word preceding it loses its tail, its last letter
a misspelling puts letters in the wrong order, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, before its final letter goes
taken as written

explanation.surface: A message containing a misspelt, highly detailed legal term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like thorough but splits as de-tailed: the word before it loses its last letter before the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram is a written communication sent by telegraph, so it is a kind of message.

clue.text: Artist rising a couple of hours before lunch?

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the letters read upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.clueFragment: a couple of hours before lunch?
blocks.note: two hours before a noon lunch is ten in the morning

explanation.surface: A painter getting up two hours before lunch, a late riser.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the time is reached by reasoning: lunch at noon, minus two hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Édouard Manet was a nineteenth-century French painter, a bridge between realism and impressionism.

clue.text: What's the last part of studies?

definitions.text: What's the last part of studies?

indicators.note: the last part of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter of the word
the 's of the contraction stands for is

explanation.surface: A quiz question asking what comes at the end of a course of studies.
explanation.walkthrough: The question answers itself: its final letter is S, so the reply reads as THE S IS, and a dissertation is also the final stage of a degree.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesis is the long dissertation submitted at the end of a degree, the culmination of years of academic work.

clue.text: Celebrity's expression of mild irritation is taken the wrong way

indicators.note: the wrong way round means read backwards, from right to left

blocks.note: 'rats!' is a mild exclamation of annoyance

explanation.surface: A famous person's muttered annoyance is misinterpreted, as in a tabloid story.
explanation.definitionFit: A star is a famous performer or public figure, the same as a celebrity in everyday usage.

clue.text: Double VAT added to small washing machines

indicators.note: one group is attached to the next in a row, building the word from parts

blocks.note: a double is a twin, an identical counterpart
a vat is a large tub
S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A tax note: VAT is charged twice on small appliances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'VAT' looks like the British sales tax, value added tax, but it is just a large tub. A twin tub is an older British washing machine with separate washing and spinning drums.
explanation.definitionFit: Twin tubs are washing machines with two drums side by side, one to wash and one to spin.

clue.text: Fools cut the top off pineapple

indicators.note: cutting off the top of a word removes its first letter

blocks.note: ananas is the French, and old English, word for pineapple

explanation.surface: Clumsy people slice the crown off a pineapple, a kitchen scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the leading A from ANANAS. Nana is British slang for a fool or idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British usage a nana is a silly person, so the plural means a group of idiots.

clue.text: Greek governors protest in numbers

indicators.note: one word is placed in the middle of the other

blocks.note: NOS is the abbreviation for numbers
a protest march

explanation.surface: Greek officials face protests from large crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' is the usual abbreviation, with its letters split open by the protest.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomarch was the governor of a nome or nomarchy, an administrative province of Greece or ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Talk about a great story

indicators.note: about here means turned around, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: gas is idle chatter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A conversation about an excellent tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talk about' looks like a phrase meaning discuss, but 'about' turns the word for chatter around.
explanation.definitionFit: A saga is a long heroic narrative, originally Norse, so it is literally an epic tale.

clue.text: Great declines overturned with investment of loan

indicators.note: something overturned is flipped upside down, so in a down entry it reads upwards
to invest is to put something inside, so one word goes into the other

blocks.note: dips are falls or drops
to loan something is to lend it

explanation.surface: A financial report: great declines reversed thanks to an investment loan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investment' and 'loan' look like finance, but investment means putting one word inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendid and great are both informal words of approval for something excellent.

clue.text: A stupid amount of Chinese food?

blocks.note: dim means slow-witted
a sum is an amount, especially of money

explanation.surface: Someone has ordered a ridiculous quantity of Chinese takeaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Dim sum are small Cantonese dumplings and snacks served in steamer baskets, a classic Chinese meal.

clue.text: Run without a partner

blocks.note: first meaning: in cricket, one run scored from a ball
second meaning: unmarried or not in a relationship

explanation.surface: Going for a jog alone, or running a business without a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a single is one run scored.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a one-run score in cricket and also describes someone who is not in a couple.

clue.text: Couple touring parts of Western Austria

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go round it, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: to couple things is to tie them together
parts played by actors are roles

explanation.surface: A pair on a holiday tour of regions of western Austria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts of' looks like it belongs with Austria; the definition is only 'of Western Austria'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tirolese is the adjective for the Tyrol, the alpine state in the west of Austria.

clue.text: Serve up some meats - a perfect meal

indicators.note: some of the words means just a part of their letters is used
in a down entry, serving something up sends it upwards, so it reads from the bottom

blocks.note: the run of letters spans three words

explanation.surface: A waiter serving some meats, an ideal dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Repast is a formal or literary word for a meal, especially a substantial one.

clue.text: The brilliance of a Welsh actor

blocks.note: first meaning: a lustrous shine
second meaning: Michael, the actor from Port Talbot

explanation.surface: Praise for the brilliant work of an actor from Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a soft glossy shine and is also the surname of the Welsh actor Michael who played Tony Blair.

clue.text: Fish identified by its angry writhing

indicators.note: writhing means twisting about, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: both words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A fish recognised by how it thrashes about in anger.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingray is a flat-bodied fish with a venomous barb on its tail.

clue.text: Don't bother with seconds of your cake, it's disgusting!

indicators.note: skipping the second, fourth and so on of the letters means only every other one is kept

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone refuses a second helping of a cake they find revolting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like a second helping, but it means every second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Yuck is an exclamation of disgust, the same reaction as calling something revolting.

clue.text: Playwright having a drink with the Queen

blocks.note: a pint, of beer usually
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cipher

explanation.surface: A dramatist sharing a drink with the monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Pinter was a Nobel-winning English dramatist, author of The Birthday Party and The Caretaker.

clue.text: Dead comedian's statements about stupid, uncultured American

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word goes round the other

blocks.note: bills are statements of charges owed
a hick is an unsophisticated rural American

explanation.surface: A late comedian's remarks about a dim-witted American yokel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Statements' looks like spoken remarks but means financial bills.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Hicks was an American stand-up comedian known for scathing satire, who died in 1994.

clue.text: Scottish girl in a boxing ring

indicators.note: boxing means enclosing as in a box, so the words close around another piece

blocks.note: taken as written
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A Scottish girl fighting in a boxing ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing ring' looks like one place, but boxing is the instruction and ring is the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Iona is a girl's given name from Scotland, taken from the Hebridean island famous for its abbey.
